hints: Look carefully at the words double-stranded and 120 nucleotides. Are all 120 nucleotides on the strand that is actually used to make the protein?
Remember the coding rule: 3 bases on the template strand make 1 mRNA codon, and 1 codon codes for 1 amino acid. How many usable bases do you really have?
walkthrough:
**Sort out how many nucleotides are actually used**

Only one of the two DNA strands is transcribed to make mRNA. So the 120 nucleotides are shared between two strands.

Usable nucleotides on one strand:
$$120 \div 2 = 60 \text{ nucleotides}$$

**Apply the triplet code rule**

The genetic code is a triplet code. It takes 3 nucleotides (1 codon) to code for 1 amino acid.

Number of codons:
$$60 \div 3 = 20 \text{ codons}$$

**Find the maximum polypeptide length**

Each codon can code for one amino acid, so 20 codons gives a maximum of 20 amino acids. We say maximum because a stop codon would shorten it, but without that information we assume all code for amino acids.

options.A: Correct and well done. 60 usable nucleotides divided by 3 per codon gives 20 amino acids.
options.B: This forgets the DNA is double-stranded. It divides all 120 by 3, but only half the nucleotides are on the transcribed strand.
options.C: This divides 120 by 2 but forgets the triplet code. 60 is the number of nucleotides, not the number of amino acids.
options.D: This assumes 1 nucleotide codes for 1 amino acid. Remember, it always takes a triplet of 3 nucleotides for 1 amino acid.
